verified_management.fact: Scientists cannot reliably predict an earthquake's exact time, place and magnitude. Long-term probabilities identify risk, not an exact event forecast.

Japan issued an earthquake early warning after sensors detected the first earthquake waves. The recorded delay was 8.6 seconds after the first P-wave was detected at the nearest station. This is detection of an event already under way, not advance prediction.
The first tsunami warning was issued at 05:49 UTC, about three minutes after the 05:46 earthquake. Initial estimates were too low and were updated. A warning can provide useful time but has limits.

Earthquake-resistant buildings and retrofitting can reduce shaking damage; coastal barriers can reduce some tsunami impacts. No measure guarantees safety. The 2011 tsunami overtopped or damaged some coastal defences.
Practised evacuation plans, clear routes, warning education and emergency supplies can help people respond. Japan reviewed disaster education and evacuation practice after 2011.

Protection changes structures or physical exposure; preparation develops plans, skills and readiness. Early warning communicates detected danger and supports prepared action. Prediction is a different claim.
